doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Piano at five, clarinet at eight, school performances
summary: Parents started him on piano to calm him, then clarinet; school assemblies brought attention and rewards.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Can I take you back for a moment — I’m wondering if there was a specific recording or incident where music got into your head. Do you remember one of the first things that made an impression on you musically, as a kid?

I was fortunate. As a kid. Well I had a different experience probably. I played piano at five years old. My parents started me playing the piano because I was a nervous kid running around. And they would take me shopping and I was so crazy I would just pull the groceries off the shelves and put them on the floor. You know I was hard to contain you know. And concentration was like a gnat, I couldn’t concentrate on anything. So when people say well give him a piano, take him — he needs discipline. He needs to be able to concentrate. So I started playing piano at the age of five and actually took piano lessons, and it helped. So my grandfather says, “Doing good.” So I was eight years old and they said, “Give him a clarinet.” He bought me a clarinet. See how that works. So I

got a clarinet. I’m playing it to this day, the clarinet. So I started playing that in elementary school. But the thing is, because I had to sit still and decipher notes on the page, that was a job for me. It was a job you know. I didn’t like it. But I concentrated and when I concentrated I got rewards. And then when I got in middle school we got — we had these different performances, we called them like assemblies where like we would play for plays and you’d play for dance shows and so I got attention because at that time I was playing first clarinet. And the girls would come up and talk to me because I was on display you know. And oh I liked that. What a way to go, you know, I’m getting attention now. So the rewards, if I practiced good and got these shows and stuff I would get accolades and whatnot, and I would get attention from the girls. I would say, “This works.” So I started playing more and practicing. Then when I got to high school I met guys that was playing bebop. Like I don’t know if you know Charles McPherson?
